subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview: The big idea of this unit is simple and joyful: when something goes wrong, we can find the mistake and fix it. That is what it means to be a problem solver. First, you learn to put steps in the right order — because a list of steps only works if the steps come in the right order (you cannot cook the anjero before you mix it). Second, you learn to find a wrong step in a list — a step that points the wrong way or has the wrong number. Third, you meet the computer word for a mistake in a program: a bug. Finding and fixing a bug is called debugging, and it is a normal, happy part of the work. A list of steps in the right order has a special name: an algorithm. a list of steps. You only need to feel it: the steps to make anjero, the steps to walk to the park, the steps to get ready for school. Every one of these is an algorithm.
learningPath: Preview the goals, key words and the tools you will use
Read the concept explainers and study the code examples
Follow the methods and worked examples
Build the activities, debug your work and play the games
Apply, explain and finish the Unit Project and Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Computing 0672 — Stage 1 Teacher & Parent Guide, Activity Sheet and Mini-Project. Teacher-directed prose was rewritten into learner-facing explainers so the unit teaches with no adult present.

outcomes: Put a short list of instructions (2-4 steps) into the right order.
Say, in their own words, why the order matters — for example, you cannot cook the anjero before you mix it.
Understand that a list of steps in the right order is called an algorithm (a list of steps).
Find the wrong step in a short algorithm — a step that goes the wrong way or has the wrong number.
Know that a mistake is called an error, and a mistake in a program is called a bug.
In ScratchJr, add a character and join Move blocks so it walks, then tap the green flag to run it.
Find and fix a bug in a short program — for example, the wrong start block or a block pointing the wrong way.
Stay cheerful about mistakes and keep trying — the heart of being a problem solver.

concepts.title: Steps in the right order (unplugged)
concepts.explanation: A job is made of steps. The steps only work if they are in the right order. A list of steps in the right order is called an algorithm — which just means “a list of steps.” Let us make anjero! What do we do first? Try it: You write 1, 2, 3, 4 in the little boxes. Do the first card together, then you can finish. Check yourself: you have to mix it first. Can you put a short set of steps into a sensible order?

concepts.title: Bugs: find and fix the mistake in a program
concepts.explanation: Programs can have mistakes too. A mistake in a program is called a bug. Finding it and fixing it is called debugging. Everyone makes bugs — even the people who make your favourite games — so a bug is nothing to worry about. It is just a puzzle to solve. A bug is just a mistake in our blocks. When we find it and fix it, we are debugging. Point to the top block: it is Start on Tap, not Start on Green Flag.
concepts.example: Find one real example of bugs: find and fix the mistake in a program around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you understand that a bug is a mistake we can fix, not a disaster? Can you try again cheerfully? Can you find one wrong block and say what it should be?

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Programs can have mistakes too. A mistake in a program is called a bug. Finding it and fixing it is called debugging. selfAssessment: I can put a short list of instructions (2-4 steps) into the right order.
I can say, in their own words, why the order matters — for example, you cannot cook the anjero before you mix it.
I can understand that a list of steps in the right order is called an algorithm (a list of steps).
I can find the wrong step in a short algorithm — a step that goes the wrong way or has the wrong number.
I can know that a mistake is called an error, and a mistake in a program is called a bug.
I can in ScratchJr, add a character and join Move blocks so it walks, then tap the green flag to run it.
I can find and fix a bug in a short program — for example, the wrong start block or a block pointing the wrong way.
I can stay cheerful about mistakes and keep trying — the heart of being a problem solver.
